function.name: requests_get
function.description: Sends a GET request to the specified URL to retrieve weather data from the Open-Meteo API. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

url.description: URL of the Open-Meteo API endpoint.

headers.description: Headers to include in the request. Each key-value pair represents a header field and its value.

Content-Type.description: The MIME type of the body of the request (used with POST and PUT requests).

Accept.description: Media type(s) that is/are acceptable for the response.

timeout.description: Maximum time in seconds to wait for the server to send data before giving up. This is a float type value.

params.description: Query parameters for the GET request.

latitude.description: Latitude of the location, positive for N and negative for S. This is a float type value.

longitude.description: Longitude of the location, positive for E and negative for W. This is a float type value.

elevation.description: Elevation in meters above sea level for the location. The default value represents no elevation downscaling.

auth.description: Authentication tuple for HTTP authentication, in the format (username, password).

cert.description: Path to the SSL client certificate file (.pem). A null value means no client certificate is used.

cookies.description: Dictionary of cookies to send with the request. Each key represents a cookie name.

proxies.description: Dictionary mapping protocol names to the URL of the proxy. Each key-value pair represents a protocol and its proxy URL.

stream.description: If True, the response should be streamed; otherwise, it should be downloaded immediately.

verify.description: Whether to verify the server's TLS certificate.

message.content:
**Java** is a high‑level, class‑based, object‑oriented programming language that was originally developed by James Gosling and his team at Sun Microsystems (now owned by Oracle) and released in 1995. It’s designed to be:

| Feature | What it means |
|---------|---------------|
| **Platform‑independent** | “Write once, run anywhere” – Java programs compile to bytecode that runs on any device with a Java Virtual Machine (JVM). |
| **Object‑oriented** | Everything is an object (except primitives), encouraging modular, reusable code. |
| **Strongly typed** | Types are checked at compile time, reducing runtime errors. |
| **Garbage‑collected** | Automatic memory management frees developers from manual memory deallocation. |
| **Secure** | JVM sandboxing, bytecode verification, and a robust security manager help protect against malicious code. |
| **Multithreaded** | Built‑in support for concurrent execution of threads. |
| **Rich standard library** | Collections, I/O, networking, GUI (Swing/JavaFX), database connectivity (JDBC), and more. |

---

### Quick History

| Year | Milestone |
|------|-----------|
| 1991 | Sun’s “Green Project” begins (Java’s predecessor, Oak). |
| 1995 | Java 1.0 released – “Write once, run anywhere.” |
| 1998 | Java 2 (J2SE 1.2) introduces Swing, Collections, and more. |
| 2004 | Java 5 (J2SE 5.0) adds generics, annotations, enums, and enhanced for‑loop. |
| 2011 | Oracle acquires Sun Microsystems. |
| 2014 | Java 8 introduces lambda expressions, streams, and the new Date/Time API. |
| 2017 | Java 9 introduces modules (Project Jigsaw). |
| 2021 | Java 17 is a long‑term support (LTS) release. |
| 2023 | Java 21 is the latest LTS release. |

---

### Typical Use Cases

| Domain | Why Java? |
|--------|-----------|
| **Enterprise applications** | Robust, scalable, and supported by mature frameworks (Spring, Jakarta EE). |
| **Android apps** | Android SDK uses Java (or Kotlin, which interoperates with Java). |
| **Web servers & microservices** | Spring Boot, Micronaut, Quarkus. |
| **Big data** | Hadoop, Spark, Flink are written in Java or Scala (runs on JVM). |
| **Desktop GUIs** | Swing, JavaFX. |
| **Embedded systems** | Java ME, Android Things. |
| **Financial services** | High‑performance trading platforms, risk engines. |

---

### A Minimal Example

```java
public class HelloWorld {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        System.out.println("Hello, Java!");
    }
}
```

Compile & run:

```bash
javac HelloWorld.java   # compiles to HelloWorld.class (bytecode)
java HelloWorld         # runs on the JVM
```

---

### Common Misconceptions

| Myth | Reality |
|------|---------|
| **Java is the same as JavaScript** | Completely different languages; Java is statically typed, compiled; JavaScript is dynamically typed, interpreted. |
| **Java is slow** | Modern JVMs use Just‑In‑Time (JIT) compilation and adaptive optimization; Java performance rivals native C/C++ in many scenarios. |
| **Java is only for desktop** | It’s widely used on servers, mobile (Android), cloud, IoT, and more. |

---

### Getting Started

1. **Install the JDK** (Java Development Kit) – e.g., OpenJDK 21 or Oracle JDK.
2. **Choose an IDE** – IntelliJ IDEA, Eclipse, VS Code (with Java extensions).
3. **Learn the basics** – syntax, control flow, OOP concepts, exception handling.
4. **Explore frameworks** – start with Spring Boot for web services or JavaFX for GUIs.
5. **Build & run** – use Maven or Gradle for dependency management and build automation.

---

### Resources

| Type | Link |
|------|------|
| Official Java SE Documentation | https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/ |
| OpenJDK Downloads | https://openjdk.org/install/ |
| Java Tutorials (Oracle) | https://docs.oracle.com/javase/tutorial/ |
| Spring Boot Guides | https://spring.io/guides |
| Java Community Process (JCP) | https://jcp.org/ |

---

**Bottom line:** Java is a versatile, mature language that powers everything from enterprise back‑ends to Android phones, thanks to its platform independence, strong typing, and rich ecosystem. Whether you’re building a web service, a desktop app, or an embedded system, Java offers a solid foundation and a vast array of libraries and frameworks to accelerate development.
